 Social Security says it's cleaning up millions of records. What that means for you.
 Ivana Pino · Senior Writer Wed, October 21, 2026 at 9:46 PM GMT+1 3 min read The Social Security Administration (SSA) said this week it has made progress in improving the accuracy of the Social Security number database.  
 The agency said it has made corrections to nearly 15% of all active Social Security numbers (SSNs) since the beginning of the Trump administration, including dates of death to records and missing citizenship information. It said the database covers approximately 330 million U.S. citizens and nearly 390 million records in total.  
 SSA said it added 17 million dates of death to records, using internal SSA systems and Department of State data. The agency said it used data from the Department of Homeland Security's Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) service, a citizenship verification tool, to update about 25 million records that lacked citizenship information.  
 "The Social Security Number database is our country's books and records," said Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano in a news release. "Accurate SSN records prevent fraud across federal programs and support the proper administration of benefits."  
 Read more: Social Security's latest COLA may fall short for retirees. Here's why. 
 What it means for your benefits or records 
 SSA has not said whether this correction has changed anyone's benefit payments or eligibility. However, maintaining accurate, up-to-date records is key to receiving the correct benefit amount.  
 Death records, for example, matter for survivor benefits, which provide financial support to family members after someone receiving or eligible for Social Security dies. 
 Read more: Social Security survivor benefits: What you'll get and how to apply 
 Payment errors have been an issue at SSA in the past. According to a July 2024 report from the Office of the Inspector General, improper payments totaled about $71.8 billion (0.84% of benefits paid from fiscal 2015 to 2022), often stemming from beneficiaries failing to report changes. 
 The Social Security Administration office in Mount Prospect, Ill. · AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh How to check your Social Security information 
 Federal and state agencies use SSA records to validate identities and prevent improper payments. SSA uses them to pay out retirement and disability benefits. 
 "It goes way beyond the check," said David Kassir, managing director of private wealth management at Manna Wealth Management. "A wrong death listing, a citizenship flag that shouldn't be there, a bad date of birth — any of those can stop your checks, cancel your Medicare, or even freeze your bank account."  
 The SSA hasn't asked the public to take any steps. Still, it could be worth logging into your online account to verify that your personal information is accurate and up to date.  
 This includes reviewing your earnings record and comparing this record with your tax records, pay stubs, and W-2s. SSA uses this data to calculate your benefit amount, so the figures must be accurate. Even a misspelled name or incorrect earnings figure can lead to issues receiving your benefits down the line or receiving the wrong amount.   
 Current beneficiaries, particularly those who may be missing a payment, can review their payment details and benefit amounts to confirm they are receiving the correct amount on time and that it's going to the right place.  
 If your earnings record is wrong, you can request a correction online , or contact Social Security directly to ask about next steps for resolving the issue.  
 "This is one of the few things in financial planning that costs nothing, takes a few minutes, and protects a check you might rely on for decades," Kassir said.
